h: Tips for groundlings and daytime visitors
p: Standing in the yard as a groundling is the classic Globe experience, just as it was in Shakespeare's day. You're right up close to the stage, actors might wander through the crowd, and the atmosphere is electric. The catch? It's open to the sky, so dress for the weather. Pack a waterproof rather than relying on a brolly, because umbrellas block everyone else's view. Comfy shoes are a must when you're on your feet for a full play.

Fancy a seat instead? The galleries give you a bench and a roof over your head, and plenty of people hire or bring a cushion. Either way, eat beforehand or grab something nearby, because a long play on an empty stomach is a test of anyone's love for the Bard.

Not catching a show? You can still visit by day for a guided tour and the exhibition, which tell the story of the original playhouse and how this one was rebuilt. The project was driven by the American actor and director Sam Wanamaker, who sadly died in 1993 before it was finished. Look up at the thatched roof, too: it was the first one allowed in London since the Great Fire of 1666.

Location-wise, you're spoilt. Tate Modern is right next door, the Millennium Bridge carries you across the river to St Paul's Cathedral, and a short walk east brings you to Borough Market and Southwark Cathedral. Bankside is made for wandering, so build in time either side of your visit.
